source_text: Γλώσσης δὲ φείδεσθαι καλόν, καὶ εὐσταθούσῃ χρῆσθαι καρδίᾳ ἐν τῇ περὶ λόγους σπουδῇ. Οὐ γὰρ χρὴ ἀλογίστως αὐτῶν ἔχοντα, κἂν ἄτοπα, ἢ τὰ ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα, ταῦτα προΐεσθαι διὰ τῆς φωνῆς· ἀλλ᾽ ἐνθυμουμένους, ὅτι εἰ καὶ πολὺ ἀφεστήκαμεν οὐρανοῦ, γινώσκειν χρή, ὅτι ἐπ᾽ ἐπηκόῳ φθεγγόμεθα Θεοῦ, καὶ ἔστι λυσιτελὲς λαλεῖν ἀπεριπτώτως. Ὥσπερ δὲ φροντίσι ψυχῆς ποικίλαις παρέπεται ὀνειράτων παντοδαπῇ φαντασίᾳ· οὕτω καὶ ἀφροσύνῃ φλυαρία συνέζευκται. Ἐπαγγελία δὲ δι᾽ εὐχῆς γινομένη, τέλος λαμβανέτω δι᾽ ἔργου. Ἀφρόνων δὲ ἴδιον, τὸ ἀποβλήτους εἶναι· σὺ δὲ ἀληθὴς ἔσο, γινώσκων ὡς πολλῷ ἄμεινον μὴ εὔξασθαί σε, μηδὲ ὑποσχέσθαι τὶ δρᾶσαι, ἢ εὐξάμενον, εἶτα παραλιπεῖν. Δεῖ δὲ παντοίως φεύγειν τὴν τῶνδε καλῶν ῥημάτων ἐπιρροήν, ὡς ἀκουσομένου θεοῦ. Τῷ γὰρ ταῦτα ἐνθυμουμένῳ πλέον οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἢ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι τῶν ἑαυτοῦ ἔργων ὑπὸ θεοῦ διαφθειρομένων. Ὥσπερ γὰρ τὰ πολλὰ ἐνύπνια μάταια, οὕτω καὶ τὰ πολλὰ ῥήματα. Φόβος δὲ Θεοῦ, ἀνθρώπων σωτήριος, σπάνιος δέ. Ὅθεν οὐ χρὴ θαυμάζειν ἀφορῶντα πρός τε πένητας συκοφαντουμένους, καὶ πρὸς δικαστὰς παραλογιζομένους. Χρὴ δὲ ἐκτρέπεσθαι τὸ τῶν δυνατωτέρων μείζονας εἶναι δοκεῖν. Κἂν γὰρ ἐκγένηται τοῦτο, ἀλλ᾽ οὖν τῶν ἐσομένων σοι φοβερῶν, οὐ ῥύσεταί σε ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν πονηρία.
thought_title: Guarding speech and vows before God
orientation: The author, continuing Solomon's voice, instructs on restraining the tongue, keeping vows through action, and fearing God rather than marveling at injustice or envying the powerful.
pass_a_gloss: It is good to spare the tongue and to use a steady heart in the effort concerning words. For one must not, holding them irrationally, even if they are absurd, or the things that have come into mind, pour them out through the voice; but reflecting that even if we have stood far away from heaven, it is necessary to know that we speak upon a listening God, and it is profitable to speak inescapably. Just as the varied concerns of the soul are attended by the all-kind fantasy of dreams; so also idle talk is yoked together with folly. And a promise made through prayer, let it receive its end through work. Of the foolish it is characteristic to be ones who cast off vows; but you be true, knowing that it is much better not to have vowed, nor to have promised to do something, than having vowed, then to neglect it. One must in every way flee the influx of such fine words, as God hearing. For to the one reflecting on these things nothing more exists than to perceive one's own works being destroyed by God. For just as many dreams are empty, so also many words. Fear of God is saving for humans, but rare. From which it is not necessary to marvel, looking at both the poor being oppressed, and judges reasoning falsely. It is necessary to turn away from the stronger ones seeming to be greater. For even if this comes to pass, yet of the fearful things coming to you, wickedness by itself will not rescue you.

choices.why: Glossary maps the idea of restraint in speech to 'empty and useless' pursuits; 'spare' captures the deliberate holding back of the tongue.
Literal rendering of the idiom; 'steady' matches the glossary's emphasis on fixed, measured disposition.
Glossary entry mandates 'idle talk' for φλυαρία; banned terms avoided.
Conveys the sudden rush of fine-sounding words; 'influx' is neutral and literal.
Covers the sense of exploitation by false accusation without importing legal jargon.
General term for moral evil; fits the context of self-deception and divine judgment.

bible_refs.note: Do not be rash with your mouth; let your heart not be hasty to utter anything before God
When you vow a vow to God, do not delay paying it; better not to vow than to vow and not pay
For in many dreams and in many words there are many vanities; but fear God
If you see oppression of the poor and perversion of justice, do not marvel at the matter
Better a poor wise youth than an old foolish king; context of power and injustice

pass_b_english: It is good to spare the tongue and to use a steady heart when you apply yourself to words. For you must not, even if thoughts are irrational or out of place, let whatever comes to mind pour out through your voice. Instead, consider that even though we stand far from heaven, we speak to a God who hears, and it is profitable to speak without stumbling. Just as varied dreams follow the soul's many cares, so idle talk is joined to folly. A promise made in prayer should be fulfilled by action. It is the mark of fools to be worthless, but you be true, knowing it is far better not to vow at all, nor to pledge any deed, than to vow and then fail. You must in every way flee the influx of such fair-sounding words, since God hears. For the one who ponders this has nothing more than to perceive his own works being corrupted by God. For as many dreams are empty, so also many words. Fear of God is the salvation of humanity, yet it is rare. Therefore you must not wonder when you see the poor being oppressed and judges reasoning falsely. You must avoid seeming greater than those who are more powerful. For even if this comes about, wickedness itself will not rescue you from the terrors that will be yours.

problems.quote: to make promises they cast off
problems.why: ἀποβλήτους means 'rejected/worthless'. It describes what the foolish are. The English makes it a trait of their promises, which they 'cast off'.
problems.fix: It is the mark of fools to be worthless (rejected); but you be true,

problems.quote: You must turn away from letting the more powerful seem greater.
problems.source_quote: Χρὴ δὲ ἐκτρέπεσθαι τὸ τῶν δυνατωτέρων μείζονας εἶναι δοκεῖν.
problems.why: The warning is not to seem greater than the more powerful. The English reverses who seems greater.
problems.fix: You must avoid seeming greater than those who are more powerful.
problems.ruling: τῶν δυνατωτέρων is a genitive of comparison: μείζονας εἶναι δοκεῖν means seeming greater than the powerful. The English has the powerful seeming greater, which reverses the sense.

edits.old: It belongs to the foolish to make promises they cast off, but you be true, knowing it is far better not to vow at all, nor to pledge any deed, than to vow and then fail.
edits.new: It is the mark of fools to be worthless, but you be true, knowing it is far better not to vow at all, nor to pledge any deed, than to vow and then fail.

edits.old: You must turn away from letting the more powerful seem greater.
edits.new: You must avoid seeming greater than those who are more powerful.

fixed: Changed 'to make promises they cast off' to 'to be worthless' to match ἀποβλήτους εἶναι (fools are characterized as rejected/worthless, not as casting off promises).

Changed 'turn away from letting the more powerful seem greater' to 'avoid seeming greater than those who are more powerful' to correct the reversed agency in ἐκτρέπεσθαι τὸ τῶν δυνατωτέρων μείζονας εἶναι δοκεῖν.

problems.quote: your own wickedness will not rescue you
problems.source_quote: οὐ ῥύσεταί σε ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν πονηρία
problems.why: καθ᾽ αὑτήν means wickedness in itself, not wickedness belonging to the hearer.
problems.fix: wickedness itself will not rescue you from the terrors that will be yours
problems.ruling: 'ἡ καθ᾽ αὑτὴν πονηρία' means wickedness by itself. 'Your own wickedness' drops that nuance and wrongly assigns the wickedness to the hearer.

edits.old: your own wickedness will not rescue you from the terrors that will be yours.
edits.new: wickedness itself will not rescue you from the terrors that will be yours.

fixed: Changed 'your own wickedness' to 'wickedness itself' to match καθ᾽ αὑτήν (by/within itself), not a possessive. The Greek means wickedness in itself will not save you, not the hearer's wickedness specifically.

last_rejected.quote: even if thoughts are irrational or out of place, let whatever comes to mind pour out through your voice
last_rejected.source_quote: Οὐ γὰρ χρὴ ἀλογίστως αὐτῶν ἔχοντα, κἂν ἄτοπα, ἢ τὰ ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα, ταῦτα προΐεσθαι διὰ τῆς φωνῆς
last_rejected.why: ἀλογίστως is how one holds words; κἂν ἄτοπα is concessive; ἢ adds a second thing not to utter. English collapses this.
last_rejected.fix: You must not thoughtlessly utter the words you hold, even if they are absurd, or whatever comes to mind.
last_rejected.ruling: The English keeps the core prohibition: don't let ἐπὶ νοῦν ἐλθόντα pass through τῆς φωνῆς. The 'even if' phrasing is awkward, but the meaning is not lost or reversed.

last_rejected.quote: For the one who ponders this has nothing more than to perceive his own works being corrupted by God.
last_rejected.source_quote: Τῷ γὰρ ταῦτα ἐνθυμουμένῳ πλέον οὐδέν ἐστιν, ἢ τὸ αἰσθάνεσθαι τῶν ἑαυτοῦ ἔργων ὑπὸ θεοῦ διαφθειρομένων.
last_rejected.why: ταῦτα means these fair words, not the warning. διαφθειρομένων means destroyed, not morally corrupted.
last_rejected.fix: For the one who dwells on these words has nothing left but to see his own works destroyed by God.
last_rejected.ruling: 'this' for ταῦτα is vague but the sense is close. διαφθειρομένων ('ruined/corrupted') is within its range, and the verse echoes Eccl 5:5, where God destroys the work.

last_rejected.why: Of judges, παραλογίζομαι means they cheat or pervert judgment, not that they reason poorly.
last_rejected.ruling: παραλογίζομαι means to reason falsely or deceive. 'Reasoning falsely' is within that range, and it still reads as judges acting dishonestly, so a reader is not misled.
